plan.title: How React Reconciliation Works
plan.summary: You will understand how React compares the new description of your screen with the previous one and changes only the parts of the real page that need updating.

prerequisites.explanation: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live tree of everything on a web page: every heading, button and text block is a node in this tree. Changing the DOM changes what you see, but each change costs the browser some work.
In React, a component is a reusable function that returns a description of a piece of the screen, such as a button or a list. Components can contain other components, forming a tree.
State is data a component remembers between updates, such as a counter value or the text typed into a box. When state changes, React re-runs the component to get a new description of the screen.

A React element is a small, plain JavaScript object describing what should appear, for example 'a <button> with the text Save'. It is only a description, not the real thing on the page. A tree of these is often called the 'virtual DOM'.

analogy.text: Imagine updating a printed seating chart for a dinner. Instead of reprinting the whole room plan, you compare the old chart with the new guest list and only change the name cards that are different. Where the analogy breaks down: React uses fixed, quick rules for comparing rather than examining every possible difference, so sometimes it rebuilds a section that a human would have kept.

plan.visualGuide: Most steps show two trees side by side: the 'Previous tree' on the left and the 'New tree' on the right, built from rounded boxes labelled with element types like <div> or <ul>. The 'Real DOM' sits as a separate tree at the bottom or far right, representing the actual page. Neutral boxes are unchanged nodes, active highlights the pair currently being compared, new marks added or updated nodes, danger marks removed nodes, old marks the outdated version, and accent is used for props, keys and state values shown as small tags on the boxes. Muted is used for parts of the tree not involved in the current step.

steps.title: Components Describe the Screen
steps.caption: Your components do not touch the page directly. They return React elements: light descriptions of what the screen should look like. Together these form a tree.

visual.description:
On the left, a code snippet: function App() returning

Hello

and . An arrow labelled 'returns' points right to a tree of three boxes:
at the top, with child boxes

'Hello' and
visual.whatChanges: The code turns into a tree of element boxes.

steps.title: First Render Builds the DOM
steps.caption: On the very first render there is nothing to compare against, so React creates a real DOM node for every element and puts them on the page.

visual.description: The element tree sits at the top. Below it, an empty area labelled 'Real DOM'. Arrows labelled 'create' go from each element box down to matching DOM node boxes, which appear in the new colour one at a time. The element tree is then labelled 'Previous tree' and slides to the left to be remembered.
visual.whatChanges: Real DOM nodes are created for every element.

steps.title: State Changes, New Tree
steps.caption: When state changes, React calls the affected components again. They return a brand-new element tree describing the updated screen.

visual.description: The Previous tree sits on the left. A small accent tag 'count: 0' on the App box changes to 'count: 1'. An arrow labelled 're-render' produces a New tree on the right, identical except the <button> text now reads 'Clicked 1'. The changed text is shown in the new colour.
visual.whatChanges: A second, new element tree appears beside the old one.

steps.title: Reconciliation Means Comparing
steps.caption: Reconciliation is the process of comparing the new tree with the previous one to work out the smallest set of real DOM changes. Rebuilding the whole page each time would be slow and would lose things like typed text and focus.

visual.description: Previous tree on the left, New tree on the right. A label 'Reconciliation' appears between them. Dashed active-coloured lines connect matching boxes pairwise, starting at the roots and moving down level by level. At the end a small box 'List of changes' appears at the bottom containing one item: 'update button text'.
visual.whatChanges: Matching nodes are paired up and one change is identified.

steps.title: Fast Rules, Not Perfect Diffing
steps.caption: Finding the absolute minimum changes between any two trees is very slow for large trees. So React uses two simple assumptions that let it compare in roughly one pass through the tree.

visual.description: A box on the left labelled 'Perfect comparison' with a tall bar labelled 'very slow'. A box on the right labelled 'React's rules' with a short bar labelled 'about one pass'. Below the right box, two accent cards appear: 'Rule 1: different type = rebuild' and 'Rule 2: keys identify list items'.
visual.whatChanges: The two rules appear as React's shortcut.

steps.title: Different Type: Replace Subtree
steps.caption: If an element at the same position changes type, for example <div> becomes <section>, React throws away the old node and everything inside it, then builds the new one from scratch. State inside is lost.

visual.description: Left: Previous tree with a <div> containing a <Counter> box with an accent tag 'state: 5'. Right: New tree with <section> at the same position containing <Counter>. The comparison line between <div> and <section> turns active, then the whole old subtree turns danger and fades out. The new subtree appears in the new colour, and the Counter tag now reads 'state: 0'.
visual.whatChanges: The old subtree is removed and a fresh one is created.

steps.title: Same Type: Update in Place
steps.caption: If the type matches, React keeps the existing node. For HTML elements it updates only the changed attributes. For components it keeps the same instance and its state, passing in the new props (inputs from the parent).

visual.description: Two pairs shown stacked. Top pair: Previous <button class='blue'> and New <button class='red'>; only the class tag flashes and changes to the new colour while the box itself stays. Bottom pair: Previous <Counter label='A'> with 'state: 5' and New <Counter label='B'>; the label tag updates in the new colour while 'state: 5' stays unchanged and neutral.
visual.whatChanges: Only the changed attribute or prop is updated; the node and state remain.

steps.title: Lists Without Keys
steps.caption: For a list of children, React by default matches them by position: first with first, second with second. Inserting an item at the start shifts every position, so React updates every item and may attach state to the wrong one.

visual.description: Previous <ul> on the left with items 'Bob', 'Cat'. New <ul> on the right with items 'Ann', 'Bob', 'Cat'. Position numbers 1, 2, 3 appear beside each item. Lines connect by position: Bob to Ann, Cat to Bob, and nothing to Cat. Each matched item flashes active and shows 'text changed'; the last 'Cat' appears in the new colour as created.
visual.whatChanges: Matching by position causes every item to be changed.

steps.title: Keys Identify Items
steps.caption: A key is a stable, unique label you give each list item, such as a database ID. React matches items by key instead of position, so it sees that only 'Ann' is new and keeps Bob and Cat, including their state.

visual.description: Same lists as the previous step, but each item has an accent key tag: key='b' Bob, key='c' Cat on the left; key='a' Ann, key='b' Bob, key='c' Cat on the right. Lines connect matching keys: b to b, c to c, both neutral. 'Ann' (key='a') appears alone in the new colour, labelled 'insert'.
visual.whatChanges: Matching switches from position to key, leaving one insertion.

steps.title: Render Phase, Then Commit
steps.caption: Work happens in two phases. In the render phase React calls components and compares trees, without touching the page. In the commit phase it applies the collected changes to the real DOM at once, so you never see a half-updated screen.

visual.description: A horizontal timeline across the canvas with two segments. Left segment 'Render phase' shows the two trees and comparison lines, with a 'List of changes' box filling up with items: 'insert Ann', 'update class'. Right segment 'Commit phase' shows the Real DOM tree; arrows from the list go into it and the affected nodes change to the new colour together.
visual.whatChanges: Collected changes are applied to the real DOM in one go.

steps.title: Fiber: Work in Small Pieces
steps.caption: Since React 16, reconciliation uses a structure called Fiber, which splits rendering into small units of work. With newer features, React can pause rendering for urgent updates like typing, then resume. The commit phase itself is never split.

visual.description: The render phase segment from the previous step is broken into small blocks labelled 'unit of work'. An accent block 'urgent: keypress' slides in between them; the remaining render blocks shift right while the urgent one completes first. At the end, the single solid 'Commit' block follows, unbroken.
visual.whatChanges: Render work is split and can be interrupted; commit stays whole.

plan.recap: Components return a tree of React elements describing the screen, not the screen itself. When state changes, React builds a new tree and reconciles it with the previous one to find what actually changed. It uses fast rules: a different type rebuilds that subtree, the same type is updated in place and keeps its state, and keys identify list items. All changes are worked out in the render phase and applied to the real DOM together in the commit phase.
